name: Felix Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate the rock breaker at a large mine, using the boom to clear oversized stone before it jams the crusher. I am 58 with a vocational certificate, but nobody learns the feel of a lodged rock from a classroom alone. I like seeing the belt move again and dislike pressure to hurry while a person may still be near the chute. My partner works at a postal sorting depot, our children are grown and living separately, and we have around five months of expenses saved on two regular wages. A few other mines are in driving range, but I have never used AI tools and prefer a radio call from somebody who sees the blockage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crusher crew faster forms are fine if they still record who checked a blockage. I would say rock breaking stays a hands-on job while the machine needs a careful operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my crusher shifts are safe in this small-change picture. Our five-month reserve and my partner's postal wage give us room if an ordinary bill arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating the rock breaker and checking the chute is clear before moving the boom. I'd record every blockage in the handover book so the next shift knows where stone caught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly comfortable about work here. I still want the crew to keep the lockout steps, which means making sure power is isolated before anybody enters the chute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made you mention lockout?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A large stone wedged at the chute mouth last month, and somebody wanted to poke it loose while the belt was live. I stopped the boom and waited for the power to be isolated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner about this scenario?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the job still pays and the postal depot still has its usual hours. We would leave our reserve alone until it was actually needed.

feel: I feel **calm about income** and attentive to safe lockout steps.

fieldNote: His **five-month reserve** and two steady wages make mild software change feel financially safe.
He returns to **lockout practice** because a recent chute blockage showed the cost of rushing.

steps.text: Keep operating the rock breaker and checking the chute

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew AI planning may change load timing before a robot can clear an awkward jam. I would ask for real shift records before anyone claims a smaller crew can manage the crusher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think tighter scheduling could take away callout pay when the crusher stops after hours. I have never used AI and would not want to be the first tester of a system beside the chute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the callout roster with actual blockage hours over the next two months. I'd try a paid screen demonstration if the new system changes the breaker schedule. I'd keep the lockout checklist in the handover book despite any electronic summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am uneasy about losing callout pay, but the base wage and my partner's job cover our bills. I would need to see the screen work before I let it set the pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the demonstration convincing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a wet-shift blockage shown from start to finish, including who checked that power was off. A tidy diagram without people and timings would tell me little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if callout pay falls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would save a little less, but the five-month reserve means we could take a breath. I would ask payroll for the numbers before making a big change at home.

feel: I feel **uneasy** about callouts while expecting ordinary bills to remain covered.

fieldNote: He wants **shift evidence** and a complete safety sequence before trusting a planning screen.
Possible **callout loss** concerns him, but base pay, partner wages and savings support an uneasy rather than anxious response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2028 can plan the crusher, while rock-breaker robots could arrive around 2031. I would ask the company for written staffing plans before it removes an operator from the chute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect robot breakers around 2031 to end many paid operator shifts, perhaps mine. Five months saved is not enough to cover the years before retirement if nearby mines buy the same machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the plant superintendent this month for the robot-test and staffing dates. I'd apply for a crusher safety inspector vacancy at another mine if one opens. I'd cut new furniture spending until the next staffing plan is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am alarmed because I still need this wage and the robot would reach my station soon. I wake up thinking about the mortgage after the reserve runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 2029 look like at the crusher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still operate the breaker if people were needed, even while AI planned loads and checked records. I would ask whether the robot tests include a person who can stop the boom before somebody enters the chute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change jobs now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for a real inspector opening, but I would not resign on a rumour. There are some mines nearby, yet they may all be buying the same equipment.

S2.quote: I would apply for a real inspector opening, but I would not resign on a rumour.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 planning changes** from the 2031 robot risk to his physical station.
The **mortgage and finite reserve** make possible operator losses distressing despite nearby mines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 thinking AI changes planning, but a human may run the breaker until robots around 2034. I would ask for paid safety posts rather than a vague promise to keep older staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I could move into inspections if a post and proper training are there. At 66 in 2034, I may still need work, so the robot date cannot simply be my retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the safety manager whether breaker operators can shadow inspectors on paid shifts. I'd enroll in a safety course if the mine pays fees and keeps my wages. I'd keep taking crusher shifts in 2032 while applying for inspector vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra years make a careful move possible. I am anxious until I see a paid opening, because I will not trade a wage for a certificate without a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to learn as an inspector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with the lockout paperwork and the actual walk around the crusher. A checklist has to match the person standing at the chute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine pays for a course but has no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would finish it only while my crusher pay continued, then apply at the other sites. I would not ask my grown children to cover our mortgage while I waited.

I would ask for **paid safety posts** rather than a vague promise to keep older staff.

At **66 in 2034**, I may still need work, so the robot date cannot simply be my retirement date.
do: Ask the **safety manager** whether breaker operators can shadow inspectors on paid shifts.
Enroll in a **safety course** if the mine pays fees and keeps my wages.
Keep taking **crusher shifts in 2032** while applying for inspector vacancies.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to check a paid inspection route.
S3.quote: A checklist has to match the person standing at the chute.
fieldNote: He grounds **inspection training** in the lockout practice he already uses at the crusher.
He keeps **2032 paid shifts** and treats a certificate as useful only with wages and a vacancy path.

steps.text: Enroll in mine-paid safety training while crusher wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2036 thinking AI may manage crusher plans while robots come around 2039. I would tell the crew ten years gives us time to calculate, not a guaranteed retirement cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I might want shorter shifts, but our mortgage will decide what is affordable. At 71 in 2039, I hope to leave the breaker, though I cannot count pension money I have not checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid breaker shifts while I can operate safely. I'd put one callout payment each month into the retirement account when callouts occur. I'd review mortgage payments with my partner each winter before reducing hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning does not make me fear next year's wages. I feel uneasy about working near the chute at 68 and about whether our savings will really carry us after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 69 and still take paid breaker or inspection shifts if we needed the money. AI might plan the loads, but capable hands-on robots would not be due until about 2039 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children be part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own housing costs. We might ask for advice on paperwork, but I would not count my grown children's wages against our mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because a robot breaker by 2031 could remove my wage while the mortgage is still due. A paid inspection course, a real vacancy and a written test schedule would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who has authority to stop the robot boom when someone walks into the chute. I will not treat that as a small technical detail.

headlineQuote: You should ask who has authority to stop the robot boom when someone walks into the chute.
portrait: Felix is a **58-year-old rock-breaker operator** at a large mine, with typical pay and a vocational certificate.
His partner's postal-depot income and **five months saved** support the household while a mortgage remains due.
He has **never used AI** and wants demonstrated safety and shift figures before trusting a new screen.
He considers **paid inspection training** if robot breakers threaten his station, while retirement stays tied to mortgage costs.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** because robot breakers around 2031 could end his wage before retirement.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid safety training**, an inspection vacancy and a written robot-test schedule.
